[Reading (Chapter 16)](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-uncertainty.html)
[Code](https://github.com/krisrs1128/data_visualization_notes/blob/main/notes/10-uncertainty.qmd)

1. Whenever we analyze a dataset, it's worth keeping in mind that our
observations could have turned out differently. Different participants might
have enrolled in the study, the sensor might be affected by measurement noise,
the author might have chosen a different word. Consequently, all inferences we
draw from data are accompanied by some degree of uncertainty.
_One of the fundamental ideas of statistics is that we can precisely measure and honestly communicate this uncertainty._

2. Yet, for most of this class, we've simply displayed the data as they are.
When most of us see a visualization like this, we don’t automatically wonder
about the hypothetical alternatives. Therefore, if we want our visual designs to
communicate uncertainty, we need clear ways of representing them graphically.

   ```{r}
   #| label: setup
   #| echo: true
   library(tidyverse)
   library(ggdist)
   library(distributional)
   library(patchwork)
   library(mgcv)
   library(tidymodels)
   library(marginaleffects)
   library(gganimate)
   theme_set(theme_classic())
   set.seed(2026)
   ```


## Frequency Framing

### Discrete Data

3. For events with discrete outcomes (e.g., win the lottery or not), it is
possible to visualize the probabilities directly. For example, if there are just
two outcomes, we can plot the probability on along a line; if there are multiple
outcomes, a stacked bar chart can achieve the same effect.

   ```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
   #| label: discrete-bars
   sample_grid <- function(p = 0.5) {
       expand.grid(seq_len(25), seq_len(25)) |>
           mutate(response = sample(0:1, n(), replace = TRUE, prob = c(1 - p, p)))
   }

   true_prob <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.4)
   outcomes <- map(true_prob, ~ sample_grid(.)) |>
       bind_rows(.id = "p") |>
       mutate(true_prob = true_prob[as.integer(p)])

   outcomes |>
       group_by(p) |>
       summarise(empirical_prob = mean(response)) |>
       ggplot() +
       geom_col(aes(as.factor(true_prob), empirical_prob)) +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0, 0.1)) +
       labs(x = "True Probability", y = "Empirical Probability")
   ```

4. However, classic studies have shown that humans are poor at judging
probabilities represented in this way [@kahneman1973psychology]. A more
effective alternative is frequency framing [@Cosmides1996, @Hoffrage2000]. The
idea is simple: create marks that represent the potential outcomes, and ensure
the frequency of the types reflects the underlying probabilities. For example,
the displays below represent the probabilities of events with 1, 10, and 40%
probability of occurring.

   ```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 2}
   #| label: freq-tiles
   #| fig-cap: A frequency framing approach to representing the probabilities of discrete outcomes.
   ggplot(outcomes) +
       geom_tile(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = as.factor(response)), col = "white", size = 0.6) +
       facet_wrap(~true_prob) +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
       scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
       coord_fixed() +
       labs(fill = "Outcome", col = "Outcome") +
       scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D9D9D9", "#595959")) +
       theme(
           axis.text = element_blank(),
           axis.ticks = element_blank(),
           axis.title = element_blank()
       )
   ```

### Continuous Data

5. How can we generalize this idea to continuous outcomes? For example, in an
upcoming election, party A might defeat party B by X%. We might believe that X
is distributed normally with mean 1.1 and standard deviation 2.4. One approach
is to visualize this using the density plot below.

   ```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3, out.width=400, dpi=300, echo = FALSE}
   #| label: density-plot
   #| fig-cap: Uncertainty in a continuous outcome shown using a probability density.
   estimate <- tibble(mean = c(1.1), sd = c(2.4))
   ggplot(estimate) +
       stat_slab(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = 0, fill = after_stat(x > 0))) +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0, 0.1)) +
       scale_fill_manual(values = c("#400D3C", "#ADD9CC")) +
       labs(x = "Forecasted Percentage Difference") +
       theme(
           axis.text.y = element_blank(),
           axis.title.y = element_blank(),
           axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
           legend.position = "none",
           panel.grid = element_blank(),
           panel.border = element_blank()
       )
   ```

6. We created this plot using the ggdist package, which extends ggplot2 with
layers for uncertainty visualization. The key ideas are in the second layer.
The `stat_slab` layer defines graphical marks for probability densities. One of
its supported `aes` arguments is `xdist`, which is expected to give an
analytical formula for a probability distribution. For example,
`dist_normal(mean, sd)` is the formula for a Gaussian distribution.  We split
the colors between parties using the `fill` argument.

   ```{r, eval = FALSE}
   #| label: density-src
   #| fig-cap: Uncertainty in a continuous outcome shown with frequency framing.
   estimate <- tibble(mean = c(1.1), sd = c(2.4))
   ggplot(estimate) +
       stat_slab(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = 0, fill = after_stat(x > 0))) +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0, 0.1)) +
       scale_fill_manual(values = c("#400D3C", "#ADD9CC")) +
       labs(x = "Forecasted Percentage Difference") +
       theme(
           axis.text.y = element_blank(),
           axis.title.y = element_blank(),
           axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
           legend.position = "none",
           panel.grid = element_blank(),
           panel.border = element_blank()
       )
   ```

7. This visualization suffers from the same limitations as directly representing
probabilities in the discrete outcome case. The frequency framing version
creates a dotplot for hypothetical outcomes at locations proportional to their
probability. It seems like a simple change, but it is often better perceived,
since judging counts is often easier than comparing areas.

   ```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3, out.width = 400, dpi=300, echo = FALSE}
   #| label: dot-plot
   #| fig-cap: A frequency framing alternative to visualizing uncertainty in a continuous outcome.
   ggplot(estimate) +
       stat_dots(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = 0, fill = after_stat(x > 0)), col = "white") +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0, 0.1)) +
       scale_fill_manual(values = c("#400D3C", "#ADD9CC")) +
       labs(x = "Forecasted Percentage Difference") +
       theme(
           axis.text.y = element_blank(),
           axis.title.y = element_blank(),
           axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
           legend.position = "none",
           panel.grid = element_blank(),
           panel.border = element_blank()
       )
   ```

8. We created this dotplot using the `stat_dots` layer from `ggdist`. Like in
ordinary ggplot2, ggdist allows us to compose layers. For example, we can create
a combined density and dot plot (this is called a rain cloud plot). The `side`
argument puts the density (the cloud) above the interval and the dots (the rain)
below it, and setting `scale = 0.5` keeps the two from overlapping.

   ```{r}
   #| label: dot-src
   #| out-width: 400
   #| fig-cap: A rain cloud plot combines density and dot views to get the best of both frequency framing and density views.
   ggplot(estimate, aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = 0, fill = after_stat(x > 0))) +
       stat_slab(scale = 0.5, side = "top") +
       stat_dots(scale = 0.5, side = "bottom", col = "white") +
       scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0, 0.1)) +
       scale_fill_manual(values = c("#400D3C", "#ADD9CC")) +
       labs(x = "Forecasted Percentage Difference") +
       theme(
           axis.text.y = element_blank(),
           axis.title.y = element_blank(),
           axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
           legend.position = "none",
           panel.grid = element_blank(),
           panel.border = element_blank()
       )
   ```

   _Exercise: What are the strengths/weaknesses of using more dots in a frequency framing visualization?_

### Multiple Inferences

9. We can compactly display the uncertainties for many inferences by stacking
dotplots or intervals. For example, in the plot below, we show chocolate quality
across many countries. More than simply describing the average quality of
chocolate bars across countries, it helps answer the more nuanced question, "If
I were in a grocery store and randomly picked a chocolate bar from country X,
what would I expect its quality to be?" That said, it can still be helpful to
include summary intervals showing the mean +/- 1 and two standard deviations
(right plot).

   ```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 8}
   #| label: cacao-dots
   cacao <- readRDS("data/cacao.rds")
   cacao_small <- cacao |>
       filter(location %in% c("Ecuador", "Australia", "Belgium", "Switzerland", "Germany"))

   p <- ggplot(cacao_small, aes(rating, reorder(location, rating))) +
       theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())
   p1 <- p + stat_dots(dotsize = .3, binwidth = .2, fill = "#6894A6")
   p2 <- p + stat_dotsinterval(dotsize = .3, binwidth = .2, fill = "#6894A6")

   p1 + p2
   ```

10. Instead of dots, we can apply the ridgeline plots we saw in the small
multiples notes. This no longer supports frequency framing, but it's much easier
to view partially overlapping density plots than dot plots.

    ```{r}
    #| label: ridgeline
    #| out-width: 400
    #| fig-cap: Uncertainty in chocolate qualitiy using ridgelines.
    p + stat_slab(height = 2, col = "black", fill = "#6894A6")
    ```

    Since these are densities, we don't necessarily need countries to have
    similar counts. When working with a larger subset of countries, this makes a
    big difference.

    ```{r, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 8}
    #| label: cacao-ridgeline
    #| fig-cap: Comparing dots with slabs for evaluating a continuous uncertainty.
    data(cacao)
    p <- cacao |>
        group_by(location) |>
        filter(n() > 12) |>
        ggplot(aes(rating, reorder(location, rating))) +
        theme(axis.title.y = element_blank())

    p1 <- p +
        stat_slab(height = 2, col = "black", fill = "#6894A6") +
        labs(title = "Legible :)")
    p2 <- p +
        stat_dots(dotsize = 0.3, binwidth = 0.2, col = "#6894A6") +
        labs(title = "Illegible :(")
    p1 + p2
    ```

11. Frequency framing is a reasonable default strategy for representing
uncertainty. However, there are many other ways to visually encode distributions
over outcomes, and they can be worth knowing for more specialized visualization
problems. For example, if we had many more countries in our chocolate bar
ratings plot, we need a more compact way of representing uncertainty. Our next
few notes explore alternatives for this and other situations.

    _Exercise: What are strengths and weaknesses of overlaying statistical summaries (e.g., slabs) on frequency framing visualizations?_

## Uncertainty in Point Estimates

12. In many cases, frequency framing plots are a good default for visualizing
uncertainty, especially for nontechnical audiences. If you have ever skimmed
through scientific publications, though, you might have noticed that the
overwhelming majority of uncertainty visualizations are based on error bars.
They give an _point estimate_ of a target quantity that's assumed to exist in a
larger population, and they use bars to represent the uncertainty in that
estimate that results from using a random sample (rather than the full
population).

13. While frequency framing gives a richer view of the distribution of possible
outcomes, there are two scenarios where error bars are hard to beat,

    - When we need to compactly represent uncertainty for many units.
    - When we want to combine them with other plots.

14. Since error bars take up so little space, they can be included in highly
information dense views. For example, the intervals cover 66, 90, and 95% of the
central area for each of 10 normal distributions.

    ```{r}
    #| label: errorbar-ci
    #\ fig-cap: Error bars can compactly visualize uncertainty in many point estimates.
    n <- 10
    estimate <- tibble(id = seq_len(n), mean = rnorm(n), sd = rgamma(n, 4, 12))
    ggplot(estimate) +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(mean, id, xmin = mean - 1.9 * sd, xmax = mean + 1.9 * sd)) +
        labs(title = "95% Confidence Intervals (Randomly Generated)")
    ```

    We created this using the `geom_errorbarh` layer, which draws horizontal error
    bars when given the center (`x`) and endpoints (`xmin` and `xmax`) of the error
    bars.

15. Since they are so compact, it is relatively easy to incorporate error bars
into other visualizations. For example, we can replace points in a scatterplot
with crosses that summarize uncertainty in each dimension.

    ```{r}
    #| label: errorbar-cross
    #| fig-width: 5
    #| fig-height: 5
    #\ fig-cap: Integrating error bars into a scatterplot visualization.
    points <- tibble(
        x = rnorm(n),
        y = rnorm(n),
        sd_x = rgamma(n, 3, 24),
        sd_y = rgamma(n, 3, 24)
    )

    ggplot(points, aes(x, y)) +
        geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = y - 1.9 * sd_y, ymax = y + 1.9 * sd_y)) +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = x - 1.9 * sd_x, xmax = x + 1.9 * sd_x)) +
        coord_fixed() +
        labs(title = "95% Error Bars")
    ```

    This was constructed by composing both horizontal `geom_errorbarh` and vertical
    `geom_errorbar` layers.

16. One difficulty with error bars is that their interpretations are not
self-evident from their appearance (they need to be included in the title or
caption to the figure). For example, 90 and 99% confidence intervals have
different meanings, and this needs to be explained clearly.

    ```{r}
    #| label: ci-levels
    #\ fig-cap: Error bar visualizations can change substantially when changing the confidence level, even when the actual uncertainty about the estimate is unchanged.
    level_compare <- tibble(mean = rnorm(1), sd = rexp(1), level = c(0.66, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99)) |>
        mutate(
            scaling = qnorm(level + 0.5 * (1 - level)),
            lower = mean - scaling * sd,
            upper = mean + scaling * sd
        )

    ggplot(level_compare) +
        geom_errorbarh(aes(mean, as.factor(level), xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
        labs(x = "CI for Mean", y = "Significance Level")
    ```

17. A variation on error bars that packs a little more information in nearly as
little space is the graded error bar. This is a type of error bar where
different levels of thickness are matched with different interpretations. In the
example below, we are simultaneously showing 90, 95, and 99% confidence
intervals for a mean.

    ```{r}
    #| label: graded-ci
    ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_pointinterval(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id)) +
        labs(title = "Graded CIs (66 and 95%)")
    ```

18. These graded error bars can be combined with distribution plots to create eye
or half-eye plots. This approach benefits from the advantages of both the
distribution and graded error approaches. From the distribution component, we
can see the full distribution of uncertainty, not simply summaries. Using the
error bar, we can tell whether specific values are above or below important
cutoffs.

    ```{r, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 14}
    #| label: halfeye-dotinterval
    p1 <- ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_halfeye(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id)) +
        labs(title = "Half Eye Plot")

    p2 <- ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_dotsinterval(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id)) +
        labs(title = "Dot Interval Plot")

    p1 + p2
    ```

19. A related approach is to fill in subsets of a distribution plot according to
more interpretable cutoffs.

    ```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 8}
    #| label: halfeye-fill
    ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_halfeye(aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id, fill = stat(level)), .width = c(0.66, 0.9, 0.95)) +
        scale_fill_brewer(na.value = "#f7f7f7")
    ```

20. Two other encodings are worth knowing, but are harder to fit into the rest of
this discussion. In interval plots, the fill opacity is used to encode
probability. It is harder to evaluate the exact probability values, but it is a
very compact representation.

    ```{r}
    #| label: interval-opacity
    p1 <- ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_interval(
            aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id, color_ramp = stat(level)),
            .width = c(0.66, 0.9, 0.95),
            col = "#64798C"
        )

    p2 <- ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_gradientinterval(
            aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id),
            fill_type = "segments",
            col = "#64798C"
        )

    p1 + p2
    ```

21. A second encoding is the complementary cumulative distribution (CCDF) plot.
It represents the probability that the data will lie above a particular value.
Some studies have found that nontechnical audiences often have better inferences
when they are presented distributional uncertainty via CCDFs [@Kay2016].

    ```{r}
    #| label: ccdf-plot
    ggplot(estimate) +
        stat_ccdfinterval(
            aes(xdist = dist_normal(mean, sd), y = id),
            col = "#64798C",
            fill = "#d4dae0"
        ) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
    ```

22. All the examples we've worked with in these notes have used the means and
standard deviations from hypothetical normal distributions. However, they can
all be created using the data itself. In this case, we directly use `x` rather
than `xdist` encoding in our `aes()`, and it will estimate the distribution from
the sample stored by `x`. For example, here are `point_interval` and `slab_eye`
intervals for a dataset `random_draws` where we draw 100 samples from 10
different gamma distributions.

    ```{r}
    #| label: gamma-draws
    random_draws <- map_dfr(
        1:10,
        ~ tibble(x = rgamma(1000, runif(1, 2, 8), runif(1, 5, 10))),
        .id = "id"
    )

    p1 <- ggplot(random_draws) +
        stat_pointinterval(aes(x, id))

    p2 <- ggplot(random_draws) +
        stat_halfeye(aes(x, id, fill = stat(level))) +
        scale_fill_brewer(na.value = "#f7f7f7")

    p1 + p2
    ```

    _Exercise: The quote below is from [@Kay2016]. Pick two of the visual representations of uncertainty we have discussed so far. Compare their precision (how accurately uncertainty can be evaluated) vs. glanceability (how much cognitive effort is required to draw a conclusion). This is a subjective evaluation, but make sure to give specific details from the visual representation to back your claims._
    > Designers should attend to the balance of precision and glanceability in representing uncertainty. Participants were divided over whether our visualizations were appropriately glanceable for a transit mobile app. While some said the new designs were easy and clear, more described feeling overwhelmed at least in the context of our experiment and the majority of commenters expressed doubts about being able to use these visualizations while walking to a bus stop.

## Hypothetical Outcomes

23. From our previous discussions, we now have a rich set of techniques for
representing uncertainty for either discrete or continuous random values. But
often, we hope to support inferences for more complex objects, like curves,
maps, or networks. How can we visualize uncertainty in these more richly
structured objects?

24. For example, in linear regression, it’s possible to visualize the uncertainty
associated with the fit using a confidence band. The guarantee is that, across
many random samples from the same population, the line will usually fall
entirely within the band.

    ```{r}
    #| label: confidence-band
    supernova <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/krisrs1128/stat679_code/main/examples/week13/supernova.csv")
    intervals <- gam(Magnitude ~ E9, data = supernova) |>
        predictions(newdata = supernova |> select(E9))

    ggplot(intervals) +
        geom_point(data = supernova, aes(E9, Magnitude)) +
        geom_line(aes(E9, estimate)) +
        geom_ribbon(aes(E9, ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
    ```

25. You may have seen these confidence bands for regression in your statistics
classes. Have you ever wondered why the band is shaped in the way that it is?
The curvature comes from the fact that there is uncertainty in both the
intercept and the slope for the fitted line. This is easy to understand by
overlaying the regression lines obtained from several versions of the same
dataset. Formally, we’ve applied the bootstrap to resample the original data,
though we could have just as well drawn from the posterior distribution of a
fitted bayesian linear regression.

    ```{r}
    #| label: bootstrap-curves
    bootstrap_curves <- function(formula, data, newdata, times = 150) {
        bootstraps(data, times = times)$splits |>
            map(analysis) |>
            map(~ gam(formula, data = .x)) |>
            map(~ as.numeric(predict(.x, newdata = newdata))) |>
            map2(seq_len(times), ~ tibble(newdata, Magnitude = .x, .draw = .y)) |>
            bind_rows()
    }

    bootstrap_curves(Magnitude ~ E9, supernova, supernova |> select(E9)) |>
        ggplot(aes(E9, Magnitude)) +
        geom_line(
            aes(group = .draw),
            col = "#d3d3d3", alpha = 0.5, size = 0.6
        ) +
        geom_point(data = supernova) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
    ```

26. We can generalize this idea to nonlinear fits. For example, below, we are
using multiple draws to represent the uncertainty of a smoothing spline
regression between supernova Magnitude and another oen of the predictor
variables. One nice aspect of showing multiple realizations is that it shows
uncertainty in the "turns" of individual curves, which is not reflected in the
confidence bands alone.

    ```{r}
    #| label: spline-bootstrap
    outcomes <- bootstrap_curves(
        Magnitude ~ s(E3, sp = c(.2)), supernova, supernova |> select(E3)
    )

    ggplot(outcomes, aes(E3, Magnitude)) +
        geom_line(
            aes(group = .draw),
            col = "#d3d3d3", alpha = 0.5, size = 0.6
        ) +
        geom_point(data = supernova) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))
    ```

27. When we show multiple outcomes overlaid like this, our attention tends to
focus on the area taken up by the multiple lines. In a true hypothetical outcome
plot, we animate each outcome one at a time. This draws attention to the
line-to-line uncertainty, rather than the area taken up by the ensemble. We can
create a hypothetical outcome version of the plots above using the `gganimate`
package. This extends ggplot to allow transitions across subsets of data (just
like faceting, but shown in a sequence over time rather than space).

    ```{r}
    #| label: hop-animate
    p <- ggplot(outcomes, aes(E3, Magnitude)) +
        geom_line(
            aes(group = .draw),
            col = "#d3d3d3", size = 1.5
        ) +
        geom_point(data = supernova) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
        transition_time(.draw) +
        ease_aes("sine-in-out")

    anim_save("gam_hypo.gif", p, renderer = gifski_renderer())
    ```

    <img src="https://krisrs1128.github.io/stat679_code/examples/week13/gam_hypo.gif" width=500/>

28. Alternatively, we can animate individual events while displaying the full
distribution in the background.

    ```{r}
    #| label: hop-context
    p <- ggplot(outcomes, aes(E3, Magnitude)) +
        geom_line(
            data = rename(outcomes, .draw2 = .draw),
            aes(group = .draw2),
            col = "#d3d3d3", alpha = 0.5, size = 0.6
        ) +
        geom_line(
            aes(group = .draw),
            col = "red", size = 1.5
        ) +
        geom_point(data = supernova) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
        transition_states(.draw)

    anim_save("gam_hypo2.gif", p, renderer = gifski_renderer())
    ```

    <img src="https://krisrs1128.github.io/stat679_code/examples/week13/gam_hypo2.gif" width=500/>

29. A somewhat less standard, but more interactive, approach would be to use
dynamic linking. Each point in the scatterplot below is one hypothetical
outcome, positioned by a PCA (week 12) of the 150 bootstrapped curves. Each
point represents one curve, and curves with similar shapes are placed next to
one another. Brushing over points highlights the corresponding fits in the panel
on the right. I've hidden coode for running the PCA and setting up the
coordinator, but it's available at the link at the start of the notebook.

    ```{r}
    #| label: hop-pca
    #| echo: false
    draw_similarity <- outcomes |>
        arrange(.draw, E3) |>
        mutate(ix = rep(1:39, 150)) |>
        select(-E3) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = ix, values_from = Magnitude)

    draw_coords <- draw_similarity |>
        recipe(~., data = draw_similarity) |>
        update_role(.draw, new_role = "id") |>
        step_normalize(all_numeric()) |>
        step_pca(all_numeric()) |>
        prep() |>
        bake(draw_similarity) |>
        mutate(.draw = row_number()) |>
        select(.draw, PC1, PC2)

    outcomes_pca <- outcomes |>
        left_join(draw_coords, by = ".draw") |>
        arrange(.draw, E3)

    write_csv(outcomes_pca, "data/hop_outcomes.csv")
    write_csv(draw_coords, "data/hop_draw_coords.csv")
    ```


```{ojs}
//| label: hop-setup
//| echo: false
path = (p) => new URL(`data/${p}`, document.baseURI).href

vg = {
  const vg = await import("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@uwdata/vgplot@0.19.0/+esm");
  const wasm = await vg.wasmConnector();
  vg.coordinator().databaseConnector(wasm);
  await vg.coordinator().exec([
    vg.loadCSV("outcomes", path("hop_outcomes.csv")),
    vg.loadCSV("draw_coords", path("hop_draw_coords.csv"))
  ]);
  return vg;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| label: hop-brush
range = vg.Selection.intersect()

vg.hconcat(
  vg.plot(
    vg.dot(
      vg.from("draw_coords"),
      {x: "PC1", y: "PC2", fill: "#4c4c4c"}
    ),
    vg.intervalXY({as: range, brush: {fill: "none", stroke: "#4d4d4d"}}),
    vg.width(300),
    vg.height(300)
  ),
  vg.plot(
    vg.line(
      vg.from("outcomes"),
      {x: "E3", y: "Magnitude", z: ".draw", stroke: "#bbb", strokeWidth: 0.6}
    ),
    vg.line(
      vg.from("outcomes", {filterBy: range}),
      {x: "E3", y: "Magnitude", z: ".draw", stroke: "black", strokeWidth: 1.5}
    ),
    vg.width(400),
    vg.height(300)
  )
)
```

30. One aspect of hypothetical outcomes is that they represent uncertainty in the
data space, not the parameter space. For example, in the regression above, we
could have simply drawn error bars for the intercept and slope parameters of the
fit. This would be a representation of uncertainty in the parameter space. The
data space representation, however, is much more evocative, and preliminary
experimental evidence suggests that this leads to better inferences in practical
applications.

31. Though we have focused on hypothetical outcomes for relatively simple
settings, the idea is applicable quite generally. For example, network
hypothetical outcome plots (NetHOPs) can be applied to graph data [@Zhang2022],
and @MacEachren2005 review how it can be used to communicate uncertainty in
maps.
